_comment: Clues and annotations authored for the grid in sample_fill_11.json. Keyed by entry id. Consumed by tools/build_authored_puzzle.py, which merges these with the fill geometry to produce puzzles/A001.js.

1-across.clue: Expectant fathers do it up and down (4)

annotation.definition: Expectant fathers do it up and down

blocks.clueFragment: Expectant fathers do it up and down
blocks.note: what a man does in a hospital corridor: he paces

annotation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart here — the whole sentence is the definition, told sideways. What an expectant father does up and down a corridor is PACE, which is also the speed he is not managing to keep. When a short clue offers no indicator and no obvious fodder, try reading it as one plain statement with a single word that fits.

blocks.note: the six letters to rearrange

annotation.walkthrough: 'Flattened' is doing two jobs at once. It is the history — Naples was bombed flat in 1943 — and it is the instruction to flatten the letters of NAPLES, which resettle as PLANES. The aircraft come out of the city's own name, and that is the whole joke.

blocks.note: the proverb says the grass is always greener over there — never here

annotation.walkthrough: The proverb does the defining. The grass is always greener somewhere else, and the word for somewhere else is THERE. Nothing is shuffled or hidden; five words with no machinery in them are usually a definition in disguise, and the sooner you try that reading the sooner you are out.

9-across.clue: What the Venus de Milo isn't (5)

annotation.definition: What the Venus de Milo isn't

blocks.clueFragment: What the Venus de Milo isn't
blocks.note: the statue lost both arms, so this is the one thing she cannot be

annotation.walkthrough: The statue has no arms, so the one word she can never be is ARMED. The pleasure is the double sense sitting inside it: armed means carrying a weapon, and it also just means having arms. Clues that define by denial are worth spotting — the answer is the thing the sentence says is missing.

10-across.clue: These porters carry stories, not bags (9)

annotation.definition: These porters carry stories, not bags
annotation.definitionNote: The clue defines the press by describing them, not by offering a synonym, so 'these porters' has to be read as a pun on re-porters rather than as hotel staff.

blocks.clueFragment: These porters carry stories, not bags
blocks.note: re-porters: they carry, but what they carry is copy

annotation.walkthrough: The answer is sitting in the clue with its disguise half off: re-PORTERS, porters of a second kind. They carry, as porters do, but what they carry is other people's stories. Nothing announces the pun — the only signal is that 'these porters' plainly cannot be the ones at the Ritz.

12-across.clue: The queen's help comes from a worker (9)

annotation.definition: The queen's help comes from a worker
annotation.definitionNote: A semi-&lit: the whole sentence defines an assistant, while only 'help' and 'worker' supply letters. In a full &lit every word would do both jobs at once.

blocks.note: to help is to assist
the crossword worker is almost always an ANT, occasionally a BEE

annotation.walkthrough: 'Help' gives ASSIST and 'worker' gives ANT — the first piece of crossword shorthand worth memorising. Together they make ASSISTANT, and the sentence you took them from is also the definition: an assistant is help from a worker. The anthill pays for both halves at once, because a queen's helper really would be an ant.

15-across.clue: The only instrument you can donate (5)

annotation.definition: The only instrument you can donate

blocks.clueFragment: The only instrument you can donate
blocks.note: the one in the church and the one on the donor card

annotation.walkthrough: Two senses are being rubbed together: the instrument in a church and the organ on a donor card. Neither is stated. The clue simply makes an absurd claim — you cannot post a piano to a hospital — and the absurdity is the signal. When a sentence says something odd about an everyday object, look for the word that leads a second life.

blocks.note: Internazionale, never spelt out on a back page
to inter is to bury
surface only — it turns two definitions into a football headline

annotation.walkthrough: Both halves define the answer. 'Milan club' is INTER, and to 'bury' is to inter. Read straight through it is an ordinary back-page headline, which is exactly what hides the seam: burying the opposition is what a good team does and what an undertaker does, and only one word means both.

17-across.clue: Delight mother with the magic word (6)

blocks.note: to please is to delight
what a parent is fishing for when a child forgets
surface only — the parent doing the fishing

annotation.walkthrough: Say please and you have done both things at once: PLEASE means to delight, and 'the magic word' is what every parent calls it. The two definitions are cause and effect, which is why the sentence sounds like ordinary family advice rather than a clue.

18-across.clue: The wolf's dinner is heard to pray (4)

blocks.note: said aloud, PRAY is PREY

annotation.walkthrough: 'Is heard to' tells you to use your ears. What the animal is doing is PRAY, and out loud that is PREY — 'the wolf's dinner'. The joke needs no unpacking once you picture it: the creature with the best reason to pray is the one about to be eaten.

1-down.clue: What Peter does when Paul gets paid (6)

annotation.definition: What Peter does when Paul gets paid
annotation.definitionNote: PETERS means 'dwindles' only inside the phrasal verb 'peters out', so the clue is leaning on that idiom rather than on the bare word.

blocks.clueFragment: What Peter does when Paul gets paid
blocks.note: rob Peter to pay Paul and Peter's money peters out

annotation.walkthrough: Rob Peter to pay Paul and Peter is the one left short — he peters out. The sentence is the definition, and the name inside it is the answer: the clue tells you who is being robbed and then makes his name the verb for it. Note the idiom carries the meaning; 'peter' alone needs its 'out'.

2-down.clue: Bruised peach goes for next to nothing (5)

blocks.note: the five letters to rearrange

annotation.walkthrough: 'Bruised' is the anagram indicator and PEACH is the fodder: five letters that resettle as CHEAP. The indicator is not decoration — bruising is exactly why fruit ends up in the reduced box, so the word that scrambles the letters is also the reason the price fell. And a peach, in the other sense, is a beauty; this one is going for nothing.

4-down.clue: Every ship needs a leader in front (10)

annotation.definition: Every ship needs a leader in front
annotation.definitionNote: A semi-&lit: the sentence as a whole describes leadership, while only 'leader' and 'ship' supply letters and 'in front' says where to put them.

blocks.note: the vessel itself
the one at the head of anything

annotation.walkthrough: Put the LEADER 'in front' of the SHIP and they run together as LEADERSHIP. The instruction is invisible because it is also the sense of the sentence, and the sentence is the definition too: what every ship needs at the front is precisely leadership.

5-down.clue: Call them what you like, they're still stars (5)

blocks.note: what you call someone is their names
the famous are big names

annotation.walkthrough: Both halves define the answer and the comma hides the seam. What you call someone is NAMES, and the stars are NAMES. Said aloud it is one fluent remark about celebrity, and the pleasure is watching 'call' change job as the second half lands.

6-down.clue: There's a bit of the president in our team (4)

blocks.note: hidden inside pre-SIDE-nt
surface only — the glue that makes it a sentence

annotation.walkthrough: 'A bit of' is the hidden-word signal, and there the answer sits, inside pre-SIDE-nt. A SIDE is a 'team'. The sentence is funny before you solve it — a bit of the president being on our team is exactly what people suspect of presidents — and that is what stops you counting letters.

7-down.clue: Our rep resents the people he speaks for (10)

blocks.note: the union man, or the one from the sales office
the word itself, lifted straight from the clue
surface only — it makes the sentence a member's complaint
surface only — the members on the other end of the grievance

annotation.walkthrough: 'Rep' is REP and 'resents' hands over RESENTS unchanged; run them together and you have REPRESENTS, which is what 'speaks for' means. The whole joke lives in the seam: the man who resents his members is, letter for letter, the man who represents them.

11-down.clue: Ground floor, and the world's your oyster (6)

blocks.note: the six letters to rearrange
surface only — the estate agent's promise, which is what puts an oyster in the sentence

annotation.walkthrough: 'Ground' is the anagram indicator: grind OYSTER up and the letters resettle as STOREY, a 'floor'. The trick worth stealing is that 'ground floor' reads as one ordinary phrase, so the instruction hides inside the definition's own scenery — and the estate agent's patter is what makes an oyster turn up in a flat.

12-down.clue: There's a row among the star guests (5)

blocks.note: hidden inside st-ARGUE-sts
surface only — the glue that makes it a caption

annotation.walkthrough: 'Among' is quietly doing the work: the answer is among the letters that follow, and st-ARGUE-sts hands it over. To 'row' — rhyming with cow — is to argue. The sentence is a tabloid caption, and the row really is inside the star guests, exactly where the story says it is.

13-down.clue: At the altar she hopes he'll change (5)

blocks.note: said aloud, ALTAR is ALTER
surface only — and the joke the sentence is actually making

annotation.walkthrough: ALTAR and ALTER sound identical, so the clue can print one and mean the other. A setter would often flag that with 'we hear'; here the pun signals itself, and the definition is simply 'change'. The joke is the sentence: the altar is exactly where a bride hopes her man will change, and he never does.

14-down.clue: Back at the pool for another circuit (4)

blocks.note: read backwards it becomes the answer

annotation.walkthrough: 'Back' is the reversal indicator and it reads as part of the scene — you are back at the pool. POOL turned round is LOOP, a 'circuit'. In a down clue the reversal runs upwards, so the P that began the word ends it.
